questions.title: Transporter for glucose entry into the enterocyte
questions.question: A newborn with severe diarrhoea has an inherited glucose/galactose malabsorption requiring a glucose- and galactose-free diet. Which transport protein is responsible for entry of glucose into the intestinal enterocyte from the lumen?

explanations.A: Incorrect. GLUT-2 mediates glucose exit across the basolateral membrane by facilitated diffusion, not apical uptake from the lumen.
explanations.B: Incorrect. GLUT-5 is the apical transporter for facilitated fructose entry, not glucose.
explanations.C: Correct. Glucose (and galactose) enter the enterocyte across the apical brush border by the sodium-dependent cotransporter SGLT1, a secondary active transport driven by the sodium gradient. A congenital defect in SGLT1 therefore causes glucose-galactose malabsorption with severe, potentially fatal diarrhoea. Glucose then leaves the cell basolaterally through GLUT-2.
explanations.D: Incorrect. SGLT2 handles glucose reabsorption in the renal proximal tubule, not intestinal uptake.
explanations.E: Incorrect. SGLT5 is not the intestinal apical glucose-galactose cotransporter responsible for this uptake.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 350, correct = c) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that SGLT1 mediates apical Na+-dependent glucose and galactose uptake and GLUT-2 mediates basolateral exit.

questions.title: Correct statement about medium-chain fatty acids
questions.question: Which statement about medium-chain fatty acids is correct?

options.A: They are more water-soluble than long-chain fatty acids
options.B: Within the enterocyte they are used for triglyceride resynthesis
options.D: They are transported in the lymph
options.E: They require emulsification before enterocyte uptake

explanations.A: Correct. Medium-chain triglycerides (6-12 carbons) are much more water-soluble than long-chain fats and are hydrolysed more rapidly. Because they are not resynthesised into triglyceride or packaged into chylomicrons, they pass directly into the portal blood. Their ready absorption makes them useful in many malabsorptive diseases.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Medium-chain fatty acids are not used for triglyceride resynthesis within the enterocyte; long-chain fatty acids are.
explanations.C: Incorrect. They are not packaged into chylomicrons, unlike long-chain fats.
explanations.D: Incorrect. They enter the portal blood, not the lymphatic (chylomicron) route.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Their water solubility lets them be absorbed without the emulsification and micelle formation long-chain fats need.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 352, correct = a) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that medium-chain triglycerides are water-soluble and pass directly into the portal blood without chylomicron packaging.

questions.title: Correct statement about iron transport and absorption
questions.question: A 47-year-old woman with heavy menses develops iron-deficiency anaemia needing iron supplements. Which statement about iron digestion and absorption is correct?

options.A: About 100 mg of iron is absorbed per day
options.B: Iron is absorbed rapidly from the small intestine
options.C: Iron is transported in the blood bound to transferrin
options.D: Iron must be oxidised from the ferrous to the ferric state for efficient absorption
options.E: Iron is transported into enterocytes by a ferroportin transporter on the apical membrane

explanations.A: Incorrect. Iron absorption is very limited, only a few milligrams per day, not 100 mg.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The rate of iron absorption is slow, tightly regulated to body need, not rapid.
explanations.C: Correct. In plasma, iron is carried bound to the beta-globulin transferrin, and excess is stored as ferritin, chiefly in hepatocytes. Absorption is slow and closely matched to requirement. Iron is taken up in the ferrous form, so ferrous compounds treat deficiency more effectively than ferric ones.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Iron is absorbed in the ferrous (Fe2+) state; it is reduced, not oxidised to ferric, for efficient uptake.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Ferroportin exports iron across the basolateral membrane; apical uptake uses the divalent metal transporter, not ferroportin.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 353, correct = c) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that plasma iron is carried on transferrin, that absorption is slow and ferrous-form dependent, and that it is stored as ferritin.

questions.title: Inhibitory neurotransmitter relaxing GI smooth muscle
questions.question: A 56-year-old man with dysphagia and regurgitation has a 'bird's beak' terminal oesophagus and manometry showing raised lower oesophageal sphincter pressure with no relaxation on swallowing (achalasia). Which is a putative inhibitory neurotransmitter responsible for relaxation of gastrointestinal smooth muscle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Dopamine acts as an excitatory transmitter here, not an inhibitory relaxant.
explanations.B: Correct. Relaxation of gastrointestinal smooth muscle follows activation of nonadrenergic, noncholinergic (NANC) enteric nerves whose inhibitory transmitters are vasoactive intestinal peptide and nitric oxide. Loss of these inhibitory neurons underlies the failure of sphincter relaxation in achalasia. Acetylcholine and substance P, by contrast, are excitatory.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Somatostatin is a paracrine secretion with many effects, not the NANC inhibitory neurotransmitter that relaxes this smooth muscle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Substance P is an excitatory neurotransmitter in the gut.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Acetylcholine is the principal excitatory transmitter causing contraction, not relaxation.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 355, correct = b) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that VIP and nitric oxide are the NANC inhibitory neurotransmitters relaxing gut smooth muscle, whose loss causes achalasia.

questions.title: Activator of trypsinogen in the duodenum
questions.question: After trypsinogen is secreted into the duodenum, it is converted to its active form, trypsin, by which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. Enteropeptidase (enterokinase), released from duodenal mucosal cells, cleaves inactive trypsinogen to active trypsin. Trypsin then activates the other pancreatic proenzymes, including chymotrypsinogen and the procarboxypeptidases, in an amplifying cascade. Its heavy glycosylation protects enteropeptidase itself from digestion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Procarboxypeptidase is itself a proenzyme activated by trypsin; it does not activate trypsinogen.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pancreatic lipase digests fat and has no role in activating trypsinogen.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chymotrypsin is produced downstream by trypsin and does not initiate the cascade.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Alkaline duodenal pH favours enzyme activity but does not by itself convert trypsinogen to trypsin.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 357, correct = a) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates the other pancreatic proenzymes.

questions.title: Bilirubin pattern in infectious (hepatocellular) hepatitis
questions.question: An 18-year-old presents two months after a tattoo with fever, right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting and jaundice. Which laboratory finding is most likely in infectious hepatitis?

options.A: An increase in plasma alkaline phosphatase
options.B: An increase in plasma bile acids only
options.C: An increase in both direct and indirect plasma bilirubin
options.D: An increase in direct bilirubin with a decrease in indirect bilirubin
options.E: A decrease in both direct and indirect plasma bilirubin

explanations.A: Incorrect. Alkaline phosphatase rises chiefly with bile-duct obstruction, not with hepatocellular disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Liver disease decreases bile-acid synthesis, and an isolated bile-acid rise does not characterise hepatitis.
explanations.C: Correct. Infectious hepatitis is a hepatocellular injury that impairs uptake, conjugation and excretion of bilirubin while damaged cells regurgitate pigment. Total bilirubin therefore rises with both conjugated (direct) and unconjugated (indirect) fractions raised, typically about equally. This mixed pattern distinguishes hepatocellular jaundice from pure obstruction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Both fractions rise in hepatocellular disease; indirect bilirubin does not fall.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Bilirubin rises, not falls, when jaundice appears.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 359, correct = c) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that hepatocellular (infectious) hepatitis raises both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin, unlike obstructive jaundice.

questions.title: Primary source of colonic gas
questions.question: A patient complains of flatulence. Gas within the colon is primarily derived from which of the following?

options.A: CO2 liberated by the interaction of bicarbonate and H+
options.C: Fermentation of undigested oligosaccharides by bacteria

explanations.A: Incorrect. CO2 from acid-bicarbonate interaction forms in the small intestine and does not accumulate as colonic gas.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Diffusion from blood accounts only for some nitrogen, not the bulk of colonic gas.
explanations.C: Correct. Colonic gas comes mainly from bacterial fermentation of undigested material, producing carbon dioxide, hydrogen and methane. Foods rich in indigestible carbohydrate, such as beans, markedly increase this production. Most of the gut's gas resides in the colon and is generated by this microbial fermentation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Swallowed air collects mainly in the stomach, not the colon.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Air trapped in food is a trivial source compared with bacterial fermentation.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 360, correct = c) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that colonic gas is produced mainly by bacterial fermentation of undigested carbohydrate.

questions.title: Form in which dietary fat enters the lymph
questions.question: A morbidly obese man has hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and type 2 diabetes. Processed dietary fat is extruded from the mucosal cells of the gastrointestinal tract into the lymphatic ducts in the form of which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Monoglycerides are luminal digestion products taken up into the cell, not the exported lymph form.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Diglycerides are digestion intermediates, not the particle secreted into lymph.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Triglycerides are resynthesised inside the enterocyte but are exported packaged within chylomicrons, not as free triglyceride.
explanations.D: Correct. Long-chain fats absorbed as monoglycerides and fatty acids are resynthesised into triglyceride inside the enterocyte and packaged, with cholesterol, phospholipid and apoprotein, into chylomicrons. These chylomicrons are extruded into the lacteals and carried in the lymph. Short- and medium-chain fatty acids instead enter the portal blood directly.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Free fatty acids (short/medium chain) enter the portal blood, not the lymph.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 369, correct = d) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that long-chain fat is exported from enterocytes as chylomicrons into the lymph, while short/medium-chain fat enters portal blood.
